author: polynoamial
text: 8/ Over 40 Diplomacy games with 82 human players involving 5,277 messages over 72 hours of gameplay, CICERO achieved more than double the average score of the other players and ranked in the top 10% of players! This is the first-ever human-level AI for Diplomacy.

author: polynoamial
text: 3 years ago my teammates and I set out toward a goal that seemed like science fiction: to build an AI that could strategically outnegotiate humans *in natural language* in Diplomacy. Today, I’m excited to share our Science paper showing we’ve succeeded! 🧵

quoted.text:
Meta AI presents CICERO — the first AI to achieve human-level performance in Diplomacy, a strategy game which requires building trust, negotiating and cooperating with multiple players. 

Learn more about #CICERObyMetaAI: https://t.co/hG2R0T2HZx https://t.co/IGw4RObA8n

author: polynoamial
text: That's because cooperative games may have many incompatible conventions, and to play well with humans an AI needs to understand these human conventions. Language is one example. Self-play RL w/o human data won't converge to using English in a cooperative game with communication.

author: polynoamial
text: The key element allowing us to beat imitation learning (IL) is to add planning, which humans do in these domains but that IL doesn't capture. By regularizing planning toward the IL policy, we keep the policy close to the human data while avoiding blunders common in IL!

author: polynoamial
text: @TheRandomMtrix The unpredictability part is already baked into the high dimensionality. The states and actions are based on ranges (probability vectors over hands) so you can have a deterministic policy in the high-dimensional space and the opponent still won't know your hand.

For the AI explanation of why that's the case, see our ReBeL poker bot paper: https://t.co/byZTE2sNNV. Basically, you can convert any imperfect-information game into a high-dimensional perfect-information game.
This makes sense. At the highest levels, poker is essentially a high-dimensional game of chess. https://t.co/wlqE2vN72H

author: polynoamial
text:
@singularity_net @nukkailab1 Despite the headline, AI did *not* beat human champions at Bridge:
1) The AI didn't bid (the hardest part!)
2) The AI didn't play with humans. Playing with adaptable humans is much harder than playing with a fixed bot

All of this info is in the article, just not the headline

author: polynoamial
text: Bridge remains an unsolved challenge for AI. I'm not working on it, but I think the team that actually beats world champions in the game deserves fair recognition for it.

author: polynoamial
text: @sharky6000 Yes I 100% agree that it's the combination that should get credit (and already does for those familiar with the research). But I think the importance of tree search to the result is underappreciated by the wider AI community.

author: polynoamial
text: @NoppadonKoo Yes! And in fact we have a recent paper showing that we can better model human chess/Go players by adding Monte Carlo tree search compared to just using supervised learning alone: https://t.co/XNMv5UX3sV
@polynoamial @hbouammar Things you never see in press releases: "hey NNs are great, but we still need GOFAI to make it work real well even with a constrained problem."

author: polynoamial
text: @hbouammar I think the level of appreciation drops the farther away someone is from the field. E.g., I think the authors of AlphaGo definitely appreciate MCTS's importance, but many people I talk to are surprised that even 6 years later raw NN's are still below top human performance in Go

author: polynoamial
text: 6 years ago today, AlphaGo beat Lee Sedol in a milestone for AI. Typically deep learning gets the credit, but it's important to know that nobody has *ever* trained a raw NN that's superhuman in Go. All superhuman Go bots require tree search. IMO planning is underappreciated in AI https://t.co/G7ycOvTefr
